source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig, Fried (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI), COLM - verification and format ablation
finding: Execution-verifying induced skills raised WebArena shopping success. Format mattered separately: program skills work better as callable actions, text skills work better when only placed in memory. Direct format comparison.
numbers: Shopping split, Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Add to memory: unverified text 32.6, verified program 36.4, verified text 39.0. Add as actions: verified program 40.1. Verification alone +4.2 (unverified text to verified program, both in memory); program-to-text conversion in memory +2.6 more; still 3.7 below ASI.
quote: the program format enables ready verification on skill correctness by executing them
limits: One website split, one model, single run per cell as reported; no variance given. Verification is a test-trajectory run, which costs extra rollouts.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 3 and 5. For a thinking schema that only places entries in the prompt, store entries as text (name, steps), not code. Verify before keeping where a test exists.

source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig, Fried (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI), COLM - Table 1 versus AWM
finding: Verified program skills beat unverified text workflows (AWM) on WebArena with the same Claude backbone, and used fewer steps. Verification is strict: only a minority of induction attempts pass.
numbers: WebArena 812 tasks, Claude: vanilla 32.7 (5.6 steps), AWM 36.3 (5.9 steps), ASI 40.4 (5.0 steps). ASI steps -15.3% vs vanilla, -10.6% vs AWM. In the induction audit, ASI programs passed verification in 15.6% of turns, AWM added a skill in 31.4% of turns (70 AWM and 58 ASI correct episodes used).
limits: Same research group family as AWM (CMU Neubig/Fried), so not an independent lab. AWM re-run with Claude by the ASI authors.
agent_relevance: Verify-before-keeping rejects most candidates (about 84% rejected here) yet improves results: fewer, checked entries beat more, unchecked ones.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory (v2) - failure ablation
finding: Storing lessons from failed attempts helped when the memory item was written as a reasoning lesson, but did not help (or hurt) memories built from success-only routines.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 39.0. Success-only to success+failure: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2, ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7. Full WebArena 684 tasks: no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, +MaTTS 51.8.
limits: Authors' own method; failure/success labels come from an LLM judge, not ground truth. Single run per cell, no variance given. Google authors using Gemini.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 7: failures are worth storing only as abstracted lessons (what to avoid, why), not as raw trajectories or routines. No head-to-head against SOAR-style hindsight relabelling exists.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank - retrieval count and judge accuracy
finding: More retrieved memory items lowered success: the best was a single item, with decline as items increased. The judge that decides success or failure could be noisy without wrecking gains.
numbers: Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: 49.7 at the best (smallest) setting, falling to 45.5 with 3 items and 44.4 with 4; 39.0 with no memory. Judge accuracy was 72.7% against ground truth; simulated judge accuracy from 100% to 50% gave success of about 47.6 to 50.6 (random-guess judge 47.6 still above 39.0 no memory).
quote: the relevance and quality of memory are more crucial than sheer quantity
limits: Figure text is garbled in the PDF; only the 3-item and 4-item values and the decline were read reliably. One site, one model. A random judge still beat no memory, so much of the gain is the lesson-writing step, not verification.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: keep the number of entries injected into the prompt very small (1 to 4). Retrieval relevance matters more than quantity (authors' words). Gap 5: a noisy self-judge is tolerable here, but only for web tasks with a cheap outcome signal.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory - empty-memory arm (DC-)
finding: The paper has a no-memory arm (DC-) with the same structured instructions and Python-use prompt but an empty cheatsheet. For Claude on AIME, most of the gain over plain baseline appears already in this arm. For GPT-4o on Game of 24, memory is the real driver.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, BL / DC- / DC-RS: AIME 2024 23.3 / 36.7 / 46.7 (DC-Cu 50.0); AIME 2025 6.7 / 23.3 / 30.0 (DC-Cu 36.7); AIME 2020-24 6.7 / 30.1 / 40.6; Math Equation Balancer 44.8 / 56.4 / 97.8 (Cu 100). GPT-4o Game of 24: 10.0 / 19.0 / 99.0; AIME 2024 20.0 / 36.7 / 40.0. About half of Claude's AIME 2024 gain (13.4 of 26.7 points under DC-Cu) comes from the prompt alone.
limits: Small test sets (AIME 30 questions per year, so one question = 3.3 points); single run; the DC- arm shares the format prompt but not the token count of memory runs. Claude Game of 24 only 12 to 14.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (first direct partial answer). Any library claim must be compared against a no-library arm that has the same instructions. Where the same prompt alone gets a large share, library credit shrinks. Gains concentrate in tasks where one reusable program solves the whole family (Game of 24, equation balancer).

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet - limits and full-history baseline
finding: Appending everything (full history) was worse than curation; retrieval alone sometimes hurt; small models gained little or inconsistently; GPQA and MMLU-Pro gains were small or negative for GPT-4o.
numbers: Claude AIME 2024: BL 23.3, DC-Cu 50.0; full-history variant reached 26.7 in the 2024 test and, in another model, fell from baseline 20.0 to 6.7. GPT-4o: GPQA-Diamond 57.1 to 57.1 (DC-RS), MMLU-Pro Engineering 53.2 to 51.2, Physics 75.6 to 75.2, retrieval-only (DR) Game of 24 6.0. Claude GPQA-Diamond 59.6 to 68.7 under DC-RS. Haiku AIME 2024 10.0 to 36.7, AIME 2025 only 13.3; Haiku GPQA 43.4 to 49.0.
limits: The pairing of the full-history numbers with models was hard to read from the PDF text; treat as direction, not size. Same lab built all arms.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 8: cumulative memory without curation dilutes and costs tokens; curation (rewriting) is needed; gains vanish on broad knowledge tasks (GPQA, MMLU-Pro) with no repeating structure.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute - predictability analysis and SWE-Features
finding: Sleep-time gain grows with how predictable the question is from the context. In an agentic software task the benefit reverses at high test-time budgets.
numbers: Predictability = log-probability of the question given the context under Llama2-70B base; Stateful GSM-Symbolic split into 5 quantile bins (GPT-4o-mini, Verbosity 0 prompt); the accuracy gap between sleep-time and plain test-time compute widens as questions become more predictable on both P1 and P2. SWE-Features: sleep-time has higher F1 at lower test-time budgets; standard test-time scaling is better at higher budgets. Authors say that with unpredictable or unrelated queries standard test-time scaling may be preferable.
quote: sleep-time compute is most effective when the queries are predictable from the context
limits: Gap 10. Predictability was measured with an external base model, so the check needs a log-prob scorer; the paper leaves 'which contexts have predictable questions' as future work. Synthetic stateful datasets built by splitting a question from its context (a context-only guessing baseline is in Appendix I).
agent_relevance: Rule for the schema: spend idle compute on a context only if one can guess the next question. Cheap proxy: have the model list likely questions and see how well they match. Untested.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute - amortisation cost model
finding: Sharing one sleep-time pass across many related queries cuts cost per query, under an assumption that test-time tokens are 10 times dearer than sleep tokens.
numbers: Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query lowered by up to 2.5x with 10 queries per context, with t = 10 cost weight for test-time tokens.
limits: The 10x token price ratio is an assumption (latency-optimised inference). The text confirms 2.5x in section 5.3; the about 5x figure in claim K16 was not found in the body.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: one sourced break-even style calculation: precompute pays when queries per context is well above 1 and test-time tokens are priced higher. For a token-priced single agent (t near 1) the saving shrinks. Not a library reuse rate.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks (v4) - self-generated skills
finding: When frontier agents wrote their own skill packs before solving, results fell below the no-skills baseline. Curated (human-written) skills helped by +18 to +25 points on the same configurations. Earlier versions of the paper reported about -1.3 (no benefit).
numbers: 87 tasks with deterministic verifiers. No skills / self-generated / curated, pass rate %: Claude Code + Opus 4.7 43.0 / 34.9 / 61.2; Codex + GPT-5.5 46.8 / 35.5 / 66.5; Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.0 / 24.5 / 60.8 (row order as printed; table text was misaligned). Self-gen deltas -8.1, -11.3, -11.5. Trajectory audit of 12 runs: in 10 of 12 on Codex and Gemini the solver never read the generated skills.
quote: Self-generated Skills land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations
limits: Self-generation was one pack written before the task, with no verification or testing, so it is not a wake-sleep loop. The reported delta changed across arXiv versions (-1.3 in an early report, -8 to -11.5 in v4 with newer models), so the figure is unstable. Effort levels differed for Claude Code (max vs high).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6: a one-shot, unverified self-written library does not help a frontier agent and costs tokens and attention. Any dreaming step must include verification and use in the solve path.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks (v4) - skill count and length
finding: Fewer, shorter, focused skills worked better than many or exhaustive ones. Direct comparison of entry format by length.
numbers: Curated gain by skills per task: 1 skill +18.0, 2-3 skills +19.0, 4 or more +10.1 pp. By complexity: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp. 13 of 87 tasks showed negative deltas (largest -7.4 pp). Overall: 18 configurations, no skills 33.9% to curated 50.5% (+16.6 pp).
limits: Human-curated, not agent-built; tasks are terminal and code-style domain tasks. Per-bucket sample sizes small. Failure patterns named: skill prescribes a heavyweight pipeline, displaces a stronger default, or points at a solver the agent cannot debug.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 8: the entry format that works is short and procedural; long documentation has near-zero effect. Give each entry applicability bounds and a cheap fallback.

source: Zheng, Fatemi, Jin, Wang et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: web agents can self-improve by discovering and honing skills
finding: A no-weights practice loop: the agent proposes a skill, runs it, an LLM reward model judges it, successful runs become code APIs, which are unit-tested and debugged. This is a dreaming analogue (self-proposed practice, keep what verifies) and it helped.
numbers: 160 exploration iterations per site with GPT-4o. WebArena average success 22.6 to 29.8 (31.8% relative); live sites (Online-Mind2Web, 4 sites) 40.2 to 56.2 (39.8% relative), with Car site 11.1 to 11.1 (0%) and Flight 11.7 to 29.4. GPT-4o-mini up to +54.3% relative using APIs from GPT-4o. Beats AutoEval on average, lower on Shopping.
limits: Verification is an LLM reward model plus execution tests, not ground truth. No no-library control with the same number of practice tokens. Web-site domain with shared structure. Single run, small live-site sets (9 Car tasks). The WebArena table text was garbled; the 22.6 to 29.8 pair is inferred from the stated 31.8%.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the first weights-free dreaming analogue with measured gain. For a thinking scaffold the open step is porting it from web APIs to reasoning steps, which have no unit test.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) - collapse and brevity bias
finding: Letting an LLM rewrite the whole memory at each step collapses it (context collapse). Itemised incremental updates by a separate reflector avoid collapse and give gains with no labels, using execution feedback.
numbers: AppWorld case: at step 60 the context held 18,282 tokens and accuracy was 66.7; at the next step 122 tokens and 57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline. ReAct + ACE averages +10.6% on agents, +8.6% on finance; without ground-truth labels ReAct + ACE +14.8% average over ReAct; vs Dynamic Cheatsheet +7.6% average in online mode. AppWorld average ReAct + ACE 59.4 vs top production agent IBM CUGA 60.3.
limits: DeepSeek-V3.1 as generator, reflector and curator; AppWorld and financial benchmarks, tasks with repeating structure. No no-playbook arm with matched tokens beyond the ReAct baseline. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7: supports append-with-merge entries over rewrite. A scaffold memory should be edited as separate small items.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) ACE - cost of adaptation
finding: Delta updates with non-LLM merging cut the cost of building the memory.
numbers: AppWorld offline: -82.3% adaptation latency and -75.1% rollouts versus GEPA. FiNER online: -91.5% latency and -83.6% token dollar cost versus Dynamic Cheatsheet.
limits: Reported cost is relative to other adaptive methods, not to a no-memory run, so it says nothing about absolute break-even.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: relative costs only; shows maintenance cost differs by about 5 to 10 times between designs, which can decide break-even more than the reuse rate.

source: Li (2026) When single-agent with skills replace multi-agent systems and when they fail - selection accuracy vs library size
finding: Choosing the right skill from a flat list stays above 90% up to about 20 skills, then falls; at 200 it is near 20%. Fits a sharp threshold curve.
numbers: Synthetic library of 200 skill templates, 8 domains, one-line descriptors. GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o, 3 seeds. Accuracy above 90% at 20 or fewer; degrades steadily beyond 30; about 20% at 200. Scaling-law fit R2 0.978 (mini) and 0.968 (4o). No-competitor libraries stay at 100% at 20 skills versus 95% with mixed similarity.
limits: Single-author preprint, two GPT models, synthetic skills and tasks where each query maps to one skill, selection by list in the prompt (not embedding retrieval). Author says more models are ongoing. The libraries are bigger and flatter than a reasoning scaffold would hold.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a rough ceiling for list-in-prompt selection is a few dozen entries; beyond that use retrieval or hierarchy.

source: Li (2026) When single-agent with skills replace multi-agent systems and when they fail - confusability and hierarchy
finding: Near-duplicate skills drive the loss, not size alone. Two-stage routing (pick a group, then a skill) recovered much of it.
numbers: Libraries of 12 to 120 skills in groups of 3 near-synonyms. Flat accuracy at 120: 45% (GPT-4o-mini) and 63% (GPT-4o). Hierarchical: 83-85% (+37 to 40 points) for mini; 72% (+9 to 10) for 4o; stable at 72 to 85% up to 120. Naive domain tree and confusability-aware tree performed alike here.
limits: Groupings coincided with domain boundaries in the design, so the two hierarchies were not really separated. Synthetic. The author's instruction-length hypothesis was not supported by the author's own test.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: library growth must be paired with dedupe and merge of near-duplicates and a routing layer. This supports a sleep step that merges entries.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs - retrieval K ablation
finding: A case bank of past successes and failures with similarity retrieval worked, with a sweet spot of about 4 retrieved cases on DeepResearcher.
numbers: Average over 7 QA sets, F1 / PM: K=0 59.9 / 72.2; K=1 63.6 / 77.9; K=2 63.7 / 78.1; K=4 64.5 / 78.5 (best); K=8 64.1 / 78.2; K=16 63.9 / 78.1; K=32 63.9 / 78.1. K=1 already gives about 80% of the F1 gain. GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (memory built over 3 iterations); case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 points on out-of-distribution sets.
limits: A plateau, not a sharp noise cost: K=32 only 0.6 F1 below the best. QA tasks with a retrieval tool. Planner GPT-4.1, executor o4-mini or o3.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: with similarity retrieval over cases the cost of too many entries is small and flat, unlike the sharp drop with flat in-prompt lists (d14) or ReasoningBank (d04). Retrieval design decides which regime you are in.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners - insights versus retrieved trajectories
finding: Extracted insights (abstract rules) and retrieved whole successful trajectories contribute separately, and together beat either; the better one depends on the task. A direct entry-format comparison (abstract rule vs worked example).
numbers: Insights-only versus retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%. Both together are higher on both tasks. Retrieval by task similarity beat random sampling by a large margin; reasoning-step similarity slightly lower. LLM-written insights beat hand-crafted ones; insights extracted only from the few-shot examples gave no advantage over ReAct.
limits: gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 era models. Authors' own method. The Table 3 cell values were misaligned in the PDF text, so only the text-quoted figures are used. HotpotQA and ALFWorld have repeated task structure.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no single best format. Keep both an abstract rule and one worked example per entry; a rule alone suits evidence-reading tasks, an example suits template-like tasks.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL - curriculum ablation across three domains
finding: Removing the short-to-long curriculum (random order of example clusters) hurt in all three domains, by very different amounts. The earlier claim used LOGO only.
numbers: Dev splits, CodeLlama-13B, full / no curriculum: LOGO 55.0 / 36.3 (-18.7); Date 77.0 / 56.6 (-20.4); TextCraft 34.12 / 28.78 (-5.3). Other ablations (LOGO, Date, TextCraft): no retry 48.3, 51.9, 30.43; no prune 52.0, 65.5, 25.26; no edit 53.3, 69.6, 27.35.
limits: Same lab, one model, dev splits only, single run. Still code domains with a verifier. 'Short to long query' is the difficulty proxy. Does not show whether a difficulty ordering beats random for reasoning-step libraries.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, partial: ordering helps in three domains but not equally. For the schema, build entries from the simplest solved items first.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO - comparison against the matched no-library solver (re-read for equal-token check)
finding: The LLM Solver (+Search) arm has no library and uses similar tokens per iteration. LILO beat it clearly only on LOGO; on REGEX and CLEVR the gap is smaller than the seed noise.
numbers: Mean test solve over 3 seeds, LLM Solver (+Search) vs LILO: REGEX 76.60 vs 77.07 (+0.47; SD 13.02 and 1.50); CLEVR 96.44 vs 96.76 (+0.32; SD 0.56 and 3.12); LOGO 37.84 vs 48.95 (+11.11; SD 6.80 and 9.46). Plain LLM Solver: 76.13, 88.67, 32.13. A typical iteration used 0.8M to 1.2M GPT tokens, with no clear difference by condition.
limits: Model was Codex-class (code-davinci-002) for most runs, not a current frontier model. Three seeds only; the LOGO gap is about 1 SD. The gap numbers are computed here from the paper table, not stated by the paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the equal-token no-library audit for LILO gives 'no clear gain on 2 of 3 domains'. Where the gain exists (LOGO), enumerative search over the library supplies it. Not repeated for frontier models.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO - token costs and runtime
finding: Cost of a wake plus sleep iteration was about 1M tokens, similar across conditions. LILO and the LLM-solver-with-search arm cost about 2x the runtime of others since they run both LLM and enumerative search.
numbers: 0.8M to 1.2M GPT tokens per training iteration (prompt plus completion) for each domain and model; nprompts per task capped at 4.
limits: Token costs are for 2023 models. Gives the build side of break-even only; the reuse side is not measured in tokens anywhere.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the build side is about 1M tokens per iteration; reuse-side data are only TroVE (3 reuses in 3,201 questions) and AWM call rate (18.5% of tasks). No paper reports tokens saved per reuse, so break-even stays unmeasured.
